_source: mixed-mode .NET binary using hidapi. The transport and the command table
are read directly out of the shipped code -- hts_send_cmd's IL and the
HTS_*_CMD static byte arrays -- so they are observed, not guessed.
What is still unconfirmed is marked with _needsVerification on the field:
the raw<->friendly value maps (which byte means 4000 Hz), because those
live in WinForms UI code rather than in the command table. Read them off
your own mouse with `hskctl get <field>` while the vendor app shows you
the real value, then fill in `values` and set status to verified.
status: partial means hskctl will talk to the device but you should
sanity-check every reading before trusting a write.

match._comment: VID and PIDs are the constants hts_init matches on. The config endpoint is identified by a vendor usage page (0xffff observed) plus a feature report -- not by interface number, which was 7 on the dongle despite the driver's 'mi_02' string.

transport._comment: hts_send_cmd: Sleep(60); hid_send_feature_report(h, tx, 65); Sleep(60); hid_get_feature_report(h, rx, 65); accept iff rx[1] == 0xA1. Byte 0 is the hidapi report-id byte and is 0 (unnumbered reports). No checksum anywhere in the command table.

commands._comment: Byte 2 is the payload length, byte 3 the opcode, byte 4 the link flag, byte 5 onwards the value. The read opcode is always the write opcode + 0x80. Commands whose opcode already has the high bit set are read-only.
commands._dpiComment: Confirmed against hardware. Payload: rx[5] active stage, rx[6] an unidentified flag, then seven stages of seven bytes each from rx[7] -- X u16be, Y u16be, then R G B. 2 + 7*7 = 51 = the response length the firmware reports in rx[2]. Writes go read-modify-write so the colours and the unmapped flag survive.
commands._sleepComment: Sleep is a sub-command of opcode 0x02: byte 6 selects 0x07 to set or 0x87 to get, and the value is a big-endian u16 at bytes 7-8.
commands._resetComment: HTS_RESET_CMD restores factory defaults. Deliberately not wired to any field -- nothing in the panel should be one keystroke away from wiping the mouse's config.
commands._linkFlagComment: linkFlag:false marks commands whose vendor function never sets byte 4. For sleep that byte carries part of the sub-command, so writing a link flag into it corrupts the packet.
commands._replyComment: The reply echoes the request: rx[2]=response length, rx[3]=opcode, rx[4]=link flag, payload from rx[5]. Crucially the firmware ACKs a packet carrying the wrong link flag and then ignores it, replying with an all-zero payload -- so an ACK is not proof of success.

charging._needsVerification: byte 5 of the battery reply; observed 0 while discharging -- confirm it reads 1 on the cable

connection._note: observed 1 on the dongle; the cable reports 0

pollingRate._note: Measured on hardware, not guessed. The register is a divisor of a 1000 Hz base clock: raw 1..6 clocked 1000/500/333/250/200/167 Hz, every point within 0.5% of 1000/raw. Raw 0 behaves as 1. This is why an enum was always going to be wrong. Note the ceiling here is 1000 Hz -- see _pollingCeiling.

debounceMs._needsVerification: read returns byte 0 of a 4-byte tuple (observed 03 0a 23 14, row 1 of the driver's 6-row table) while the write takes a row index -- the two are not the same number, so writing is disabled until the table is modelled

activeDpiStage._note: observed 1; rx[6] is a second flag whose meaning is not established, so it is not mapped

dpiStage1._note: X axis of stage 1. Writes confirmed on hardware: 800, 1200 and 400 each read back correctly through read-modify-write.

_pollingCeiling: The dongle clocked a 1000 Hz base during calibration, so no divisor reaches the 4000 Hz this model is sold on. 4K mode is presumably enabled elsewhere -- a separate command, a dongle mode, or a hardware switch -- and has not been located in the driver yet.
